```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

Individual differences estimated by a model, such as the variance of a
random slope, are often read as differences between the people. They can
also come from the model or from how the data are arranged. This article
shows a case where people who are all the same appear to differ in how fast
they change.

```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Data

Two hundred people are each observed twice, one year apart, starting at
ages between 0 and 3. Everyone follows the same course, rising from 0 at age
0 towards 5, quickly at first and then more slowly. The measurements have a
little error:

```{r data}
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
startage <- runif(n, 0, 3)
dat <- data.frame(id = rep(1:n, each = 2), occasion = rep(0:1, n))
dat$age <- startage[dat$id] + dat$occasion
dat$y <- 5 * (1 - exp(-dat$age)) + rnorm(nrow(dat), 0, 0.1)
```

Plotted by occasion, as a two-wave study often is, people seem to differ:
some change a lot between the two occasions and some hardly at all, and those
who start lower change more.

```{r byoccasion}
ggplot(dat[dat$id <= 30, ], aes(occasion, y, group = id)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

Plotted by age, they all lie on one curve:

```{r byage}
ggplot(dat[dat$id <= 30, ], aes(age, y, group = id)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

# Two models

A linear growth model on the occasions has a starting level and a slope for
each person. The measurement error is fixed to its true standard deviation,
which two occasions per person cannot separate from the rest:

```{r linear}
datocc <- data.frame(id = dat$id, time = dat$occasion, y = dat$y)
mlinear <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'y', latentNames = 'eta',
  LAMBDA = 1, DRIFT = 0, DIFFUSION = 0, CINT = 'slope',
  MANIFESTMEANS = 0, MANIFESTVAR = 0.1)
flinear <- ctFit(datocc, mlinear, cores = 2)
summary(flinear)$popsd
summary(flinear)$rawpopcorr
```

The slopes differ a lot between people, and they are almost perfectly
negatively correlated with the starting levels: where a person starts
predicts how fast they change.

A model on age, with time running from age 0 for everyone, describes the
shape of the course instead. Its process has an auto effect, which slows the
growth as the level rises. Each person gets a row at age 0 with nothing
observed, so that the starting value refers to age 0 for everyone. The
starting value and the intercept still vary over people:

```{r dynamic}
datage <- data.frame(id = dat$id, time = dat$age, y = dat$y)
start <- data.frame(id = 1:n, time = 0, y = NA)
datage <- rbind(start, datage)
datage <- datage[order(datage$id, datage$time), ]
mdynamic <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'y', latentNames = 'eta',
  LAMBDA = 1, CINT = 'cint', MANIFESTMEANS = 0, MANIFESTVAR = 0.1)
fdynamic <- ctFit(datage, mdynamic, cores = 2)
summary(fdynamic)$popmeans
summary(fdynamic)$popsd
```

The auto effect and intercept are close to the -1 and 5 of the process, and
almost no differences between people remain. Both models fit the same
observations, so their log likelihoods can be compared:

```{r loglik}
c(linear = logLik(flinear), dynamic = logLik(fdynamic))
```

The differences between people in the first model came from fitting a
straight line to a curve, with each person observed on a different part of
it.

# What follows

An estimated random effect means the model needs it, which can be because the
people differ, or because the model leaves something out that varies
between them. Here that was age. The same happens when cohorts of
different ages are pooled, or when the time scale of a study (occasions,
weeks since enrolment) is not the one the process follows. A model with a
time scale and a form of change closer to the process leaves less to explain
by differences between people.
